title: Biggest Triangle Perimeter From Sticks
statement:
You get the lengths of some sticks in sticks. Pick three of them to build a triangle with positive area, so the three sticks must not lie flat on one line.

Return the largest perimeter you can build, or 0 if no three sticks form such a triangle.

examples.why: The three longest sticks, 10, 9 and 5, already work: 10 < 9 + 5.
20 is longer than any two others combined, so it cannot be used. 8, 7 and 6 work.
1 + 2 = 3, so the sticks lie flat. A flat triangle has no area and does not count.

hints: Three lengths a ≤ b ≤ c make a real triangle exactly when a + b > c. The other two inequalities hold automatically.
Sort the sticks. If you fix the longest side c, which two other sticks give you the best chance and the biggest perimeter?
Fix c and use the two sticks just below it in sorted order. If even they fail, no smaller pair can work with that c, so drop c and try the next one down.

explain.intuition:
Sort the sticks from longest to shortest. For a chosen longest side c, the best partners are the two next-longest sticks: they give the largest sum, so they are the most likely to beat c, and they also give the largest perimeter.

If those two fail (b + a ≤ c), every other pair below them is even shorter and fails too, so c can never be the longest side. Move on to the next stick. The first triple that works is the answer, because every later triple is made of shorter sticks.
steps: For each i from 0 to n − 3, look at sticks[i], sticks[i + 1], sticks[i + 2].
If sticks[i] < sticks[i + 1] + sticks[i + 2], return their sum.
pitfalls: Using ≤ in the triangle test. Equality means the sticks lie flat with zero area, like [1, 2, 3].
Always taking the three longest sticks. In [20, 6, 7, 8] the 20 must be skipped.
Checking only one inequality without sorting first. a + b > c is enough only when c is the longest of the three.

solutions.title: Try every triple
solutions.idea: Check all three-stick combinations and keep the largest valid perimeter.

solutions.title: Sort and scan neighbouring triples
solutions.idea: Sorted descending, the best partners for any longest side are the next two sticks. The first neighbouring triple that works is the answer.

followups: Count how many triples form a valid triangle. Why does that need two pointers instead of neighbours?
If all lengths are distinct and at most 10⁹, at most how many sticks can there be with no valid triangle? (Think Fibonacci.)
